description: I'm a Year 13 student from Dubai interested in computer science, AI, and software development, with experience in Python, web development, and graphic design. We're currently a team of two students from GEMS Founders School Al Barsha, united by our interest in technology and innovation. Our goal is to combine our skills and creativity to develop practical solutions to real-world challenges.
summary: MarsPath is an interactive Mars atlas and mission planner for the Martian Map challenge. We paired NASA Mars Trek imagery with elevation grids and published science targets so explorers can choose a destination, compare traverses and see what supports each route. In our Jezero example, the shortest outbound route is 2.80 km. Prioritizing science recommends a 6.59 km route through a published delta outcrop. The atlas shows terrain coverage, modelled conditions and an independent return leg, then packages the plan as a printable Mission Brief and GeoJSON. We built it to make trade-offs and uncertainty visible when planning an exploration mission.
details:
What we built

  • We built MarsPath to make the Martian Map challenge approachable for students, educators and mission-planning enthusiasts. You can explore real orbital imagery and fourteen named destinations, choose a start, destination and waypoints, then compare routes and inspect the science along them.

How MarsPath plans routes

  • We use NASA Mars Trek for global and regional imagery. A TypeScript worker runs A* over numerical terrain on Mars, respecting no-data cells and a selected modelled slope limit. The app uses a 20 m Mars 2020 CTX terrain grid at Jezero, a native 20.23 m CTX window at Oxia and 0.25° MOLA cells for coarse global routes. If the terrain cannot resolve a connection, the atlas can report a separately labelled geographic estimate.
  • The interface uses Next.js static export, React and OpenLayers and runs on Vercel.

Source code: View MarsPath on GitHub

Jezero case study

  • In the Jezero Delta Investigation case, Shortest recommends 2.80 km outbound while Science first selects 6.59 km and reaches the published D-tcl outcrop. That adds 3.78 km and reuses the same four accepted candidates.
  • Distance, modelled terrain costs and missed science objectives can affect ranking. The independent return is 2.88 km. A Mission Brief and GeoJSON preserve the assumptions, paths, scientific context and sources.

Science layers and mission tools

  • Environmental views include elevation, geology, mineral observations, apparent thermal inertia, an MCD 6.2 climatology snapshot and a published radiation scenario. The Jezero comparison leaves these environmental layers as context. Explicit climate preferences can affect other comparisons when coverage supports them.
  • Archived Perseverance MEDA readings retain their time and product IDs. Mission Planner also estimates geometric daylight and terrain line of sight to a hypothetical station.

Limits and next steps

  • The science and model limits travel with the result. Resolution varies, some spans are unassessed and alignment accuracy can be unknown. Individual radiation exposure, communications reliability and rock-scale hazards remain unassessed. MarsPath is a research and education tool. Next steps could include verified ice evidence and additional regional terrain where the data supports them.

Super Intelligence (SI) disclosure

  • Our team set the direction for MarsPath and made the final decisions about what went into the app and demo. We used OpenAI Codex to help us compare implementation and editorial ideas, research sources, check our scientific analysis, write and debug code, and refine the text, interface and share graphics. Codex also helped us edit the demo and develop the code that synthesized the original music and sound effects. The demo shows screen recordings of the working MarsPath app and credited Mars mission imagery. The app uses documented measurements, published numerical data and deterministic calculations. Our use of AI was limited to developing the project and producing the demo. We credit the synthesized audio and AI assistance in the demo description and MP4 metadata, and explain how we processed and checked the scientific data in the MarsPath Methodology.
